newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: RBNZ forecasts NZ inflation has peaked.
newsitem.headline: RBNZ forecasts NZ inflation has peaked.

text.p: New Zealand's annual underlying inflation has peaked, the Reserve Bank of New Zealand said in its six monthly economic projections published on Thursday.

The annual inflation rate is projected to fall from 2.4 percent in December 1996 to 2.2 percent in the March 1997 year and to 1.2 percent in 1998 and 1.1 percent in 1999 before rising to 2.0 percent in the March 2000 year.
In the bank's previous forecasts in December it forecast inflation would peak at at annual rate of 2.3 percent in the September 1996 year and the December 1996 year.
RB Governor Don Brash said inflation would shortly fall and then start to decline rapidly as a result of a prolonged period of firm monetary conditions.
He said the appreciation of the New Zealand dollar had had a muted affect on inflation.
"Accordingly, we propose to continue operating policy towards an overall level of monetary conditions which is unchanged from that announced on December 17, 1996.

"We expect to maintain this stance until we can be confident that, after an easing, inflation would still turn down towards the middle of the (0-3 percent) target range in a clear and sustained manner."

Brash said there was little prospect of inflation falling below the bottom of the range. Brash said inflation in the non-tradeables sector continued to dominate. The new forecasts take account of the new minimum wage introduced by the coalition government formed in December.

The bank said its estimate of inflation in the March 1997 quarter (0.5 percent) was only slightly higher than previously but the projection for the June quarter has been revised up significantly to 0.5 percent.
Inflation is still expected to decline during 1997 and 1998 as the fall in import prices and labour costs took effect.
The bank's stronger growth forecasts suggest renewed pressures on capacity in 1998 resulting in a rebound in inflationary pressures later in the forecast period.

Brash said recent economic data was moderately encouraging, and the bank would continue to work on the basis that a one percent appreciattion in the exchange rate would lead in due course to a 0.3 percent fall in inflation.

He said the short-term path for inflation could be rather different if there was a different mix in conditions possibly as a result of rising concern about the current account deficit. That could produce a risk of a lower exchange rate and its pass- through effects on inflation.
